claim: Conserved ATP-dependent chromatin remodelers establish and maintain genome-wide chromatin architectures of regulatory DNA during cellular lifespan.
source: Conserved ATP-dependent chromatin remodelers establish and maintain genome-wide chromatin architectures of regulatory DNA during cellular lifespan, but the temporal interactions between remodelers and chromatin targets have been obscure.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract that references established knowledge about chromatin remodelers.

claim: Chromatin-bound remodelers display notably higher diffusion than nucleosomal histones.
source: Chromatin-bound remodelers display notably higher diffusion than nucleosomal histones, and strikingly fast dissociation kinetics with 4–7 s mean residence times.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, specifically in Figure 6 showing MSD plots and diffusion coefficients.

claim: Chromatin remodelers have strikingly fast dissociation kinetics with 4–7 s mean residence times.
source: Chromatin-bound remodelers display notably higher diffusion than nucleosomal histones, and strikingly fast dissociation kinetics with 4–7 s mean residence times.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from slow-tracking experiments presented in Figure 4.

claim: Enhanced dynamics of chromatin remodelers require ATP binding or hydrolysis by the catalytic ATPase.
source: These enhanced dynamics require ATP binding or hydrolysis by the catalytic ATPase, uncovering an additional function to its established role in nucleosome remodeling.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from ATPase mutant studies presented in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: Multiple remodelers can repeatedly occupy the same promoter region on a timescale of minutes.
source: Kinetic simulations show that multiple remodelers can repeatedly occupy the same promoter region on a timescale of minutes, implicating an unending 'tug-of-war' that controls a temporally shifting window of accessibility for the transcription initiation machinery.
evidence: This claim is supported by kinetic simulations based on measured parameters, as shown in Figure 7.

claim: Gene promoters in budding yeast contain nucleosome-depleted regions (NDRs), approximately 150 base-pair stretches of DNA that are depleted of nucleosomes.
source: In the budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae, gene promoters contain nucleosome-depleted regions (NDRs), approximately 150 base-pair stretches of DNA that are depleted of nucleosomes (Yuan, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Yuan, 2005.

claim: NDRs are flanked by well-positioned +1 and −1 nucleosomes.
source: NDRs are flanked by well-positioned +1 and −1 nucleosomes, with the +1 nucleosome overlapping the transcription start site (TSS) in yeast (Albert et al., 2007; Yuan, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Albert et al., 2007 and Yuan, 2005.

claim: The +1 nucleosome overlaps the transcription start site (TSS) in yeast.
source: NDRs are flanked by well-positioned +1 and −1 nucleosomes, with the +1 nucleosome overlapping the transcription start site (TSS) in yeast (Albert et al., 2007; Yuan, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Albert et al., 2007 and Yuan, 2005.

claim: ATP-dependent chromatin remodelers are key trans-acting factors in establishing and maintaining nucleosome organization around genes.
source: ATP-dependent chromatin remodelers are key trans-acting factors in establishing and maintaining nucleosome organization around genes (Becker and Workman, 2013; Rando and Winston, 2012; Zhang et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Becker and Workman, 2013; Rando and Winston, 2012; Zhang et al., 2011.

claim: Chromatin remodeling enzymes utilize DNA translocation as the fundamental mechanism to restructure DNA-histone contacts within nucleosomes.
source: As specialized members of the superfamily 2 (SF2) translocases, chromatin remodeling enzymes share a highly conserved ATPase motor that utilizes DNA translocation as the fundamental mechanism to restructure DNA-histone contacts within nucleosomes.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about chromatin remodeling mechanisms.

claim: Chromatin remodelers are classified into four sub-families: SWI/SNF, CHD, ISWI, and INO80.
source: They are further classified into four sub-families based on sequence homology of the catalytic ATPase and possession of shared components, namely the SWI/SNF [Switch defective/sucrose non-fermenting], CHD [Chromodomain helicase DNA-binding], ISWI [Imitation switch], and INO80 [Inositol requiring 80] sub-families.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about chromatin remodeler classification.

claim: RSC and SWI/SNF mobilize the +1 and −1 nucleosomes away from the NDR relative to the TSS to promote proper engagement of transcription initiation machinery.
source: RSC and SWI/SNF mobilize the +1 and −1 nucleosomes away from the NDR relative to the TSS to promote proper engagement of transcription initiation machinery (Ganguli et al., 2014; Klein-Brill et al., 2019; Kubik et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ganguli et al., 2014; Klein-Brill et al., 2019; Kubik et al., 2018.

claim: RSC assists NDR formation for the majority of yeast genes.
source: Specifically, RSC assists NDR formation for the majority of yeast genes, and the consequence of conditional RSC inactivation is a global loss of transcription (Brahma and Henikoff, 2019; Ganguli et al., 2014; Kubik et al., 2018; Yen et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Brahma and Henikoff, 2019; Ganguli et al., 2014; Kubik et al., 2018; Yen et al., 2012.

claim: Conditional RSC inactivation results in a global loss of transcription.
source: Specifically, RSC assists NDR formation for the majority of yeast genes, and the consequence of conditional RSC inactivation is a global loss of transcription (Brahma and Henikoff, 2019; Ganguli et al., 2014; Kubik et al., 2018; Yen et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Brahma and Henikoff, 2019; Ganguli et al., 2014; Kubik et al., 2018; Yen et al., 2012.

claim: INO80 and ISW2 reposition the +1 and −1 nucleosomes towards the NDR in vivo.
source: Both ISW2 and INO80 remodelers reposition the +1 and −1 nucleosomes towards the NDR in vivo, which is important for suppressing yeast cryptic transcription via noncanonical TSS usage (Klein-Brill et al., 2019; Kubik et al., 2019; Whitehouse et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Klein-Brill et al., 2019; Kubik et al., 2019; Whitehouse et al., 2007.

claim: INO80 and ISW2 are important for suppressing yeast cryptic transcription via noncanonical TSS usage.
source: Both ISW2 and INO80 remodelers reposition the +1 and −1 nucleosomes towards the NDR in vivo, which is important for suppressing yeast cryptic transcription via noncanonical TSS usage (Klein-Brill et al., 2019; Kubik et al., 2019; Whitehouse et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Klein-Brill et al., 2019; Kubik et al., 2019; Whitehouse et al., 2007.

claim: INO80 and ISW2 are implicated in DNA replication.
source: Furthermore, INO80 and ISW2 are implicated in DNA replication (Au et al., 2011; Lee et al., 2015; Vincent et al., 2008) and INO80 in DNA damage repair (Morrison et al., 2004; van Attikum et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Au et al., 2011; Lee et al., 2015; Vincent et al., 2008.

claim: INO80 is implicated in DNA damage repair.
source: Furthermore, INO80 and ISW2 are implicated in DNA replication (Au et al., 2011; Lee et al., 2015; Vincent et al., 2008) and INO80 in DNA damage repair (Morrison et al., 2004; van Attikum et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Morrison et al., 2004; van Attikum et al., 2004.

claim: CHD1 and ISW1 act primarily in the gene body where they maintain proper nucleosome spacing and density relative to the +1 nucleosome.
source: The second group of remodelers, CHD1 and ISW1, act primarily in the gene body where they maintain proper nucleosome spacing and density relative to the +1 nucleosome.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge about CHD1 and ISW1 function.

claim: CHD1 and ISW1 actions are coupled to transcription elongation by interacting with the elongating polymerase.
source: Their actions are coupled to transcription elongation by interacting with the elongating polymerase to maintain nucleosome density and thus suppress cryptic initiation within the gene body (Cheung et al., 2008; Radman-Livaja et al., 2012; Smolle et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Cheung et al., 2008; Radman-Livaja et al., 2012; Smolle et al., 2012.

claim: The catalytic subunits of six major chromatin remodeling complexes were tagged at the C-terminus with HaloTag by engineering the endogenous loci.
source: We tagged the catalytic subunits of six major chromatin remodeling complexes, RSC, SWI/SNF, CHD1, ISW1 (ISW1a, and ISW1b), ISW2, and INO80 at the C-terminus with the self-labeling HaloTag by engineering the endogenous loci and expressed the fusion proteins as the sole source under natural promoter control.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used in the study.

claim: The HaloTag fusion proteins were localized in the nucleus.
source: The fusion proteins were localized in the nucleus and did not display detectable cleavage of the tag by SDS-PAGE (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: The HaloTag fusion proteins did not display detectable cleavage of the tag by SDS-PAGE.
source: The fusion proteins were localized in the nucleus and did not display detectable cleavage of the tag by SDS-PAGE (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: No phenotypes were observed for all strains containing tagged constructs.
source: Furthermore, no phenotypes were observed for all strains containing tagged constructs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The majority of H2B molecules (79.4 ± 1.9%) are slow-moving with average D of 0.026 µm2s−1.
source: We found that the majority of H2B molecules (79.4 ± 1.9%) are slow-moving with average D of 0.026 µm2s−1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A) consistent with incorporation into chromatin, whereas most of the chromatin-free Halo-NLS molecules show greatly increased diffusivity (D ~ 5 µm2s−1) (Ranjan et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Chromatin-free Halo-NLS molecules show greatly increased diffusivity (D ~ 5 µm2s−1).
source: We found that the majority of H2B molecules (79.4 ± 1.9%) are slow-moving with average D of 0.026 µm2s−1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A) consistent with incorporation into chromatin, whereas most of the chromatin-free Halo-NLS molecules show greatly increased diffusivity (D ~ 5 µm2s−1) (Ranjan et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ranjan et al., 2020.

claim: Chromatin remodelers exhibit a slow Dbound fraction (average 0.036 ± 0.007 to 0.067 ± 0.004 µm2s−1).
source: Compared to H2B, chromatin remodelers exhibit a slow Dbound fraction (average 0.036 ± 0.007 to 0.067 ± 0.004 µm2s−1) as would be expected for molecules associated with largely immobile chromatin (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The Dbound values of chromatin remodelers are ~2-fold higher than H2B.
source: However, as discussed later, the Dbound values are ~2-fold higher than H2B.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of experimental data.

claim: Chromatin remodelers exhibit a chromatin-free fraction whose Dfree values (0.464 ± 0.043 to 1.014 ± 0.024 µm2s−1) are ~10-fold higher than Dbound.
source: Furthermore, we also observed a separable chromatin-free fraction whose Dfree values (0.464 ± 0.043 to 1.014 ± 0.024 µm2s−1) are ~10-fold higher, but distinctly lower than the Dfree for Halo-NLS, indicating that our imaging regime captures essentially the full range of potential diffusive behaviors for this family.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from fast-tracking experiments.

claim: The Dfree values show an inverse correlation with the estimated total molecular weights of chromatin remodeling complexes.
source: In addition, the Dfree values show an inverse correlation with the estimated total molecular weights of chromatin remodeling complexes, consistent with expectations that the tagged catalytic subunits are associated within larger complexes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The majority of RSC molecules are associated with chromatin (66.0 ± 1.1%).
source: We found that the majority of both RSC and SWI/SNF molecules are associated with chromatin (RSC: 66.0 ± 1.1%; SWI/SNF: 55.9 ± 1.3%) (Figure 1D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The majority of SWI/SNF molecules are associated with chromatin (55.9 ± 1.3%).
source: We found that the majority of both RSC and SWI/SNF molecules are associated with chromatin (RSC: 66.0 ± 1.1%; SWI/SNF: 55.9 ± 1.3%) (Figure 1D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: INO80 exhibits Fbound value of 48.3 ± 0.2%.
source: INO80 and ISW2 exhibit Fbound values of 48.3 ± 0.2% and 34.8 ± 1.0%, respectively (Figure 1F,G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: ISW2 exhibits Fbound value of 34.8 ± 1.0%.
source: INO80 and ISW2 exhibit Fbound values of 48.3 ± 0.2% and 34.8 ± 1.0%, respectively (Figure 1F,G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: CHD1 shows Fbound value of 47.8 ± 4.9%.
source: The two remodelers show comparable Fbound values (CHD1: 47.8 ± 4.9%; ISW1a/b: 52.0 ± 1.1%) (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: ISW1a/b shows Fbound value of 52.0 ± 1.1%.
source: The two remodelers show comparable Fbound values (CHD1: 47.8 ± 4.9%; ISW1a/b: 52.0 ± 1.1%) (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The Isw1 catalytic subunit is shared by two distinct chromatin remodeling complexes called ISW1a and ISW1b.
source: However, the catalytic subunit Isw1 is shared by two distinct chromatin remodeling complexes called ISW1a and ISW1b (Vary, et al., 2003), in addition to potentially un-complexed Isw1 catalytic subunit (Tsukiyama et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Vary et al., 2003 and Tsukiyama et al., 1999.

claim: The ISW1a complex localizes near the transcription start and end of genes.
source: The ISW1a complex localizes near the transcription start and end of genes, whereas the ISW1b complex occupies more mid-coding regions (Morillon et al., 2003; Smolle et al., 2012; Yen et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Morillon et al., 2003; Smolle et al., 2012; Yen et al., 2012.

claim: The ISW1b complex occupies more mid-coding regions.
source: The ISW1a complex localizes near the transcription start and end of genes, whereas the ISW1b complex occupies more mid-coding regions (Morillon et al., 2003; Smolle et al., 2012; Yen et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Morillon et al., 2003; Smolle et al., 2012; Yen et al., 2012.

claim: ISW1b (Ioc4-Halo) complex exhibits higher Fbound (55.5 ± 2.6%) compared to ISW1a (Ioc3-Halo) complex (39.6 ± 0.0%).
source: The gene-body acting ISW1b (Ioc4-Halo) complex exhibits higher Fbound compared to ISW1a (Ioc3-Halo) complex (ISW1b: 55.5 ± 2.6%; ISW1a: 39.6 ± 0.0%) (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C,D.

claim: The Log(D) histograms of all imaged chromatin remodelers display less distinct bound and free populations compared to H2B histones and HaloTag protein.
source: Unlike the two well-separated Gaussian distributions for H2B histones and HaloTag protein (Figure 3A), the Log(D) histograms of all imaged chromatin remodelers display less distinct bound and free populations, with a noticeable fraction showing an intermediate range of diffusion coefficients (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: The population of transitioning trajectories is more prominent for remodelers (from 20.9 ± 2.5% to 30.2 ± 1.5%) compared to free HaloTag (10.4 ± 0.7%) and H2B histone (7.1 ± 2.1%).
source: It is striking that the population of transitioning trajectories is more prominent for remodelers (from 20.9 ± 2.5% to 30.2 ± 1.5%) compared to free HaloTag (10.4 ± 0.7%) and H2B histone (7.1 ± 2.1%), (Figure 3C–I, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C–I and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D–E.

claim: Comparable frequencies were observed for remodeler dissociation (bound to free transition: 45.3 ± 1.3 to 50.24 ± 0.01%) and association (free to bound: 49.76 ± 0.01 to 54.7 ± 1.3%).
source: We observed comparable frequencies for remodeler dissociation (bound to free transition: 45.3 ± 1.3 to 50.24 ± 0.01%) and association (free to bound: 49.76 ± 0.01 to 54.7 ± 1.3%), indicating that there is little bias in the direction of state transitions (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Transient but frequent chromatin interactions are characteristic of the six remodeling complexes.
source: We concluded that transient but frequent chromatin interactions are characteristic of the six remodeling complexes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on transitioning trajectories.

claim: RSC exhibits a stable-binding fraction (fsb) of 27 ± 2% with a lifetime (τsb) of 5.0 ± 0.7 s.
source: The stable-binding subpopulations (fsb) of RSC (27 ± 2%) and SWI/SNF (24 ± 6%) display strikingly short lifetimes (RSC: 5.0 ± 0.7 s; SWI/SNF 4.4 ± 1.2 s) (Figure 4A,B), consistent with a previous measurement for the Rsc2 subunit of RSC (Mehta et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: SWI/SNF exhibits a stable-binding fraction (fsb) of 24 ± 6% with a lifetime (τsb) of 4.4 ± 1.2 s.
source: The stable-binding subpopulations (fsb) of RSC (27 ± 2%) and SWI/SNF (24 ± 6%) display strikingly short lifetimes (RSC: 5.0 ± 0.7 s; SWI/SNF 4.4 ± 1.2 s) (Figure 4A,B), consistent with a previous measurement for the Rsc2 subunit of RSC (Mehta et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: INO80 exhibits a stable-binding fraction (fsb) of 20 ± 3% with a residence time (τsb) of 3.7 ± 0.8 s.
source: Similarly, INO80 and ISW2 exhibit stable-binding fractions (fsb 20 ± 3% and 13 ± 3%, respectively) and similarly short residence times (τsb 3.7 ± 0.8 s and 4.9 ± 2.2 s, respectively) (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: ISW2 exhibits a stable-binding fraction (fsb) of 13 ± 3% with a residence time (τsb) of 4.9 ± 2.2 s.
source: Similarly, INO80 and ISW2 exhibit stable-binding fractions (fsb 20 ± 3% and 13 ± 3%, respectively) and similarly short residence times (τsb 3.7 ± 0.8 s and 4.9 ± 2.2 s, respectively) (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: CHD1 exhibits a stable-binding fraction (fsb) of 15 ± 3% with a dwell time (τsb) of 7.2 ± 3.3 s.
source: For gene body-acting remodelers, CHD1 and ISW1 complexes exhibit stable-binding fractions (fsb 15 ± 3% and 19 ± 2%, respectively) and short dwell times (τsb 7.2 ± 3.3 s and 5.6 ± 1.3 s, respectively) (Figure 4E,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: ISW1 complexes exhibit a stable-binding fraction (fsb) of 19 ± 2% with a dwell time (τsb) of 5.6 ± 1.3 s.
source: For gene body-acting remodelers, CHD1 and ISW1 complexes exhibit stable-binding fractions (fsb 15 ± 3% and 19 ± 2%, respectively) and short dwell times (τsb 7.2 ± 3.3 s and 5.6 ± 1.3 s, respectively) (Figure 4E,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: ISW1b shows 2.5-fold higher residence times compared to ISW1a (τsb 5.9 ± 2.5 s and 2.2 ± 1.0 s, respectively).
source: Interestingly, ISW1b shows 2.5-fold higher residence times compared to ISW1a (τsb 5.9 ± 2.5 s and 2.2 ± 1.0 s, respectively) with comparable stable-binding fractions (Figure 4—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1G.

claim: The stable-binding average residence time increased by ~2-fold (from 4.9 ± 2.2 to 9.7 ± 3.1 s) for the Isw2K215R mutant.
source: We found that the stable-binding average residence time increased by ~2-fold (from 4.9 ± 2.2 to 9.7 ± 3.1 s) for the Isw2K215R mutant (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Increased residence time (from 5.6 ± 1.3 to 9.1 ± 3.6 s) was observed for the Isw1K227R mutant.
source: Similarly, we observed increased residence time (from 5.6 ± 1.3 to 9.1 ± 3.6 s) for the Isw1K227R (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The two ATPase-dead Chd1 mutants both showed increased stable-binding residence times (Chd1K407R from 7.2 ± 3.3 to ~52 s; Chd1D513N from 7.2 ± 3.3 to 16.1 ± 7.3 s).
source: The two ATPase-dead Chd1 mutants both showed increased stable-binding residence times (Chd1K407R from 7.2 ± 3.3 to ~52 s; Chd1D513N from 7.2 ± 3.3 to 16.1 ± 7.3 s) (Figure 5E,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E,F.

claim: After chromatin association, the mutant ATPases exhibit slower dissociation rate.
source: In all, our results indicate that after chromatin association, the mutant ATPases exhibit slower dissociation rate (the reciprocal of residence time), consistent with previous genome-wide ChIP and biochemical studies (Fitzgerald et al., 2004; Gelbart et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and citations to Fitzgerald et al., 2004; Gelbart et al., 2001.

claim: Chromatin-bound remodelers exhibit ~2-fold higher mobility than H2B histone.
source: Importantly, chromatin-bound remodelers exhibit ~2-fold higher mobility than H2B histone, as revealed by the average MSD plot and the distribution of individual D values of each trajectory under fast-tracking (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A,B.

claim: The mean Rc values are substantially higher for remodelers compared to the global mean measured for H2B.
source: The mean Rc values are also substantially higher for remodelers compared to the global mean measured for H2B (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Three mutants Isw2K215R, Isw1K227R, Chd1K407R harboring substitutions in the catalytic ATPase Walker A motif display strikingly lower diffusivity.
source: Three mutants Isw2K215R, Isw1K227R, Chd1K407R harboring substitutions in the catalytic ATPase Walker A motif responsible for ATP binding display strikingly lower diffusivity as revealed by the average MSD plot of stably bound molecules, which approaches or substantially overlaps the global H2B curve (Figure 6D–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D–F.

claim: Chd1D513N bearing a substitution in the Walker B motif of Chd1 shows no substantial changes in the average MSD curve and apparent D values for stably bound trajectories compared to wildtype.
source: Surprisingly, Chd1D513N bearing a substitution in the Walker B motif of Chd1 shows no substantial changes in the average MSD curve and apparent D values for stably bound trajectories compared to wildtype as measured by slow-tracking (Figure 6F,H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6F,H.

claim: Isw2D312N exhibits an approximately two-fold increase in its residence time compared to wildtype.
source: As expected for a mutation in the catalytic ATPase, the Isw2D312N mutant exhibits an approximately two-fold increase in its residence time compared to wildtype (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The ATP-bound state may be adequate to induce enhanced diffusion on chromatin as part of the mechanism of target search by remodeling enzymes.
source: Because the Walker B motif is important for ATP hydrolysis (via coordinating Mg2+ ion and a water molecule), but not for ATP binding (Singleton et al., 2007; Walker et al., 1982; Figure 5A), this result suggests that the ATP-bound state may be adequate to induce enhanced diffusion on chromatin as part of the mechanism of target search by remodeling enzymes.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data and citations to Singleton et al., 2007; Walker et al., 1982.

claim: RSC binding is the most widespread (Ntargets = 3702).
source: Accordingly, RSC binding is the most widespread (Ntargets = 3702), SWI/SNF binds only a small subset (Ntargets = 466), and INO80 (Ntargets = 1646) and ISW2 (Ntargets = 1802) each bind to approximately a third of all yeast promoters (Kubik et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kubik et al., 2019.

claim: SWI/SNF binds only a small subset (Ntargets = 466).
source: Accordingly, RSC binding is the most widespread (Ntargets = 3702), SWI/SNF binds only a small subset (Ntargets = 466), and INO80 (Ntargets = 1646) and ISW2 (Ntargets = 1802) each bind to approximately a third of all yeast promoters (Kubik et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kubik et al., 2019.

claim: INO80 (Ntargets = 1646) and ISW2 (Ntargets = 1802) each bind to approximately a third of all yeast promoters.
source: Accordingly, RSC binding is the most widespread (Ntargets = 3702), SWI/SNF binds only a small subset (Ntargets = 466), and INO80 (Ntargets = 1646) and ISW2 (Ntargets = 1802) each bind to approximately a third of all yeast promoters (Kubik et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kubik et al., 2019.

claim: RSC shows substantial occupancy (30 ± 7.3%) at stably bound chromatin targets.
source: RSC shows substantial occupancy (30 ± 7.3%) at stably bound chromatin targets, despite its short residence time (τsb) of 5.0 ± 0.7 s.
evidence: This claim is based on calculations using measured kinetic parameters.

claim: SWI/SNF exhibits the highest occupancy (94 ± 41%) among the four remodelers.
source: SWI/SNF exhibits the highest occupancy (94 ± 41%) among the four remodelers, consistent with the highest raw ChEC signals reported for Swi3 (Kubik et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is based on calculations using measured kinetic parameters and is consistent with a citation to Kubik et al., 2019.

claim: INO80 displays substantial occupancy (25 ± 9.7%) at its targets.
source: Comparable to RSC, INO80 displays substantial occupancy (25 ± 9.7%) at its targets while ISW2 displays a lower occupancy (11 ± 7.2%).
evidence: This claim is based on calculations using measured kinetic parameters.

claim: ISW2 displays a lower occupancy (11 ± 7.2%).
source: Comparable to RSC, INO80 displays substantial occupancy (25 ± 9.7%) at its targets while ISW2 displays a lower occupancy (11 ± 7.2%).
evidence: This claim is based on calculations using measured kinetic parameters.

claim: At promoter regions targeted by multiple remodelers, the occupancy by any one remodeler is strikingly high.
source: Average time trace simulations of stably bound occupancies for each of the four remodelers over several hundred seconds (Figure 7B) show that at promoter regions targeted by multiple remodelers such as genes in 'cluster IV' enriched for RSC and INO80 (Kubik et al., 2019), the occupancy by any one remodeler is strikingly high, and more than one remodeler can simultaneously engage a promoter repeatedly over several minutes (Figure 7C; see also Figure 7—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This claim is based on simulations using measured kinetic parameters, as shown in Figure 7B,C and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: More than one remodeler can simultaneously engage a promoter repeatedly over several minutes.
source: Average time trace simulations of stably bound occupancies for each of the four remodelers over several hundred seconds (Figure 7B) show that at promoter regions targeted by multiple remodelers such as genes in 'cluster IV' enriched for RSC and INO80 (Kubik et al., 2019), the occupancy by any one remodeler is strikingly high, and more than one remodeler can simultaneously engage a promoter repeatedly over several minutes (Figure 7C; see also Figure 7—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This claim is based on simulations using measured kinetic parameters, as shown in Figure 7C and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: All imaged remodelers show stable and transient residence times of 4–7 s and 0.4–0.7 s, respectively.
source: Comparable to reported values for the Rsc2 subunit of RSC and the yeast transcription factors, Ace1 and Gal4 (Donovan et al., 2019; Mehta et al., 2018), all imaged remodelers show stable and transient residence times of 4–7 s and 0.4–0.7 s, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and citations to Donovan et al., 2019; Mehta et al., 2018.

claim: The effect of mutating the DNA-binding domain of CHD1 monomer results in a threefold reduction in the τsb value (from 7.2 ± 3.3 to 2.4 ± 0.7 s).
source: Furthermore, the effect of mutating the DNA-binding domain of CHD1 monomer (Ryan et al., 2011; Tran et al., 2000) results in a threefold reduction in the τsb value (from 7.2 ± 3.3 to 2.4 ± 0.7 s) (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C,D and citations to Ryan et al., 2011; Tran et al., 2000.

claim: Five tested ATPase-dead mutants (for ISW2, ISW1, CHD1) show twofold or greater increase in their stable-binding residence times.
source: Importantly, the fast dissociation rates of remodelers are facilitated by ATP hydrolysis. Five tested ATPase-dead mutants (for ISW2, ISW1, CHD1) show twofold or greater increase in their stable-binding residence times (Figure 5C–F), highlighting a new role of for ATP-utilization in coupling nucleosome remodeling to rapid enzyme dissociation from chromatin.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C–F.

claim: Remodelers undertake small translocation steps with remodeling rates of a few bp/sec.
source: Biochemical studies have shown that remodelers undertake small translocation steps with remodeling rates of a few bp/sec (Blosser et al., 2009; Deindl et al., 2013; Harada et al., 2016; Qiu et al., 2017; Sabantsev et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Blosser et al., 2009; Deindl et al., 2013; Harada et al., 2016; Qiu et al., 2017; Sabantsev et al., 2019.

claim: With an enzymatic rate of 2 bp/s for ISWI, an ISWI stable-binding event would allow octamer sliding by roughly 12 bp.
source: For example, with an enzymatic rate of 2 bp/s for ISWI (Blosser et al., 2009), an ISWI stable-binding event would allow octamer sliding by roughly 12 bp, which is within range of in vivo nucleosome position changes after conditional inactivation of RSC, SWI/SNF, INO80, and ISW2 (Ganguli et al., 2014; Kubik et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a calculation based on cited enzymatic rates and is consistent with citations to Ganguli et al., 2014; Kubik et al., 2019.

claim: Mutations in the ISW1, ISW2, and CHD1 Walker A motif substantially decreases in vivo mobility.
source: We further showed that this enhanced mobility is dependent on the ATPase domain. Mutations in the ISW1, ISW2, and CHD1 Walker A motif implicated in nucleotide binding (Singleton et al., 2007) substantially decreases in vivo mobility.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and a citation to Singleton et al., 2007.

claim: Mutations in the CHD1 and ISW2 Walker B motif displays a milder decrease of its chromatin mobility.
source: Further analysis of mutations in the CHD1 and ISW2 Walker B motif, implicated in ATP hydrolysis [but not ATP binding] (Singleton et al., 2007), displays a milder decrease of its chromatin mobility, suggesting that nucleotide binding is largely sufficient for promoting diffusion for the two remodelers.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and a citation to Singleton et al., 2007.

claim: RSC and Drosophila ISWI remodelers undergo ATP hydrolysis-dependent translocation on ssDNA and dsDNA in vitro.
source: In addition, RSC and Drosophila ISWI remodelers undergo ATP hydrolysis-dependent translocation on ssDNA and dsDNA in vitro (Saha et al., 2005; Whitehouse et al., 2003), with processivities of 20–70 bp/translocation event (Fischer et al., 2007; Saha et al., 2005; Sirinakis et al., 2011; Whitehouse et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Saha et al., 2005; Whitehouse et al., 2003; Fischer et al., 2007; Sirinakis et al., 2011.

claim: The absence of any change in ISW1 chromatin-bound mobility upon treatment with a general transcription inhibitor thiolutin rules out transcription per se as a source of enhanced remodeler diffusion.
source: Finally, the absence of any change in ISW1 chromatin-bound mobility upon treatment with a general transcription inhibitor thiolutin rules out transcription per se as a source of enhanced remodeler diffusion (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Chromatin remodelers use the catalytic ATPase not only for nucleosome remodeling but also to enhance target search kinetics by promoting 1D diffusion on chromatin and rapid detachment after reaction.
source: In all, our results suggest that chromatin remodelers use the catalytic ATPase not only for nucleosome remodeling but also to enhance target search kinetics by promoting 1D diffusion on chromatin and rapid detachment after reaction.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on ATPase mutants and their effects on mobility and dissociation.

claim: About half of promoters genome-wide harbor at least two distinct remodelers that harbor nucleosome pushing and pulling activities relative to the NDR.
source: Yeast promoter regions can be classified into different groups enriched either for no remodeler or a combination of RSC, SWI/SNF, INO80, and ISW2, with about half of promoters genome-wide harboring at least two distinct remodelers that harbor nucleosome pushing and pulling activities relative to the NDR (Kubik et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kubik et al., 2019.

claim: At promoter regions where opposing remodelers bind, a consecutive 'tug-of-war' between the pushing and pulling activities is expected.
source: At promoter regions where opposing remodelers bind, we expect a consecutive 'tug-of-war' between the pushing and pulling activities, in which successive engagements would ultimately result in fine-tuning the steady-state nucleosome position, with the final outcome dependent on remodeler occupancy and nucleosome remodeling activity.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the experimental data and known remodeler activities.

claim: The average promoter occupancy of the yeast PIC is in the range of 10%.
source: In a related study (Nguyen et al., 2021), the average promoter occupancy of the yeast PIC that forms upstream and overlapping the +1 nucleosome was found to be in the range of 10%, that is on the same order of magnitude but lower than three of four remodelers examined.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Nguyen et al., 2021.

claim: A full PIC lasts only several seconds before dissociation from chromatin.
source: Similar to chromatin remodelers, a full PIC lasts only several seconds before dissociation from chromatin, but the average promoter is vacant for ~100 s before PIC reformation.
evidence: This is a statement based on the related study mentioned (Nguyen et al., 2021).

claim: The average promoter is vacant for ~100 s before PIC reformation.
source: Similar to chromatin remodelers, a full PIC lasts only several seconds before dissociation from chromatin, but the average promoter is vacant for ~100 s before PIC reformation.
evidence: This is a statement based on the related study mentioned (Nguyen et al., 2021).

claim: An independent study from the Verrijzer laboratory found that the Drosophila Brahma (BRM) remodeler also displays dependence on ATP utilization by the catalytic ATPase for dynamic mobility and remodeler dissociation in live Drosophila cells.
source: It is notable that an independent study from the Verrijzer laboratory (Tilly et al. 2021) found that the Drosophila Brahma (BRM) remodeler also displays dependence on ATP utilization by the catalytic ATPase for dynamic mobility and remodeler dissociation in live Drosophila cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Tilly et al. 2021.
